OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Is there an absolute constant $K$ such that, for every $C>0$, if $n$ is sufficiently large then $n$ has at most $K$ divisors in $(n^{1/2},n^{1/2}+C n^{1/4})$. 
#887: [ErRo97]
number theory | 
divisors
A question of Erdős and Rosenfeld [ErRo97], who proved that there are infinitely many $n$ with $4$ divisors in $(n^{1/2},n^{1/2}+n^{1/4})$, and ask whether $4$ is best possible here. They also proved that, if $n$ is large enough depending on $C$, then $n$ has at most $1+C^2$ divisors in $(n^{1/2},n^{1/2}+C n^{1/4})$. 
Chan [Ch14] has resolved this when $n$ is a square, proving that if $n$ is a square then $n$ has at most $5$ divisors in\[[ n^{1/2}-n^{1/4}(\log n)^{1/7}, n^{1/2}+n^{1/4}(\log n)^{1/7}].\]In [Ch15] Chan further proves that if $n=(N-a)(N-b)$ for some $0\leq a\leq b\leq \exp((\log n)^{2/7})$ then $n$ has at most $18$ divisors in\[[ n^{1/2}-n^{1/4}(\log n)^{1/14}, n^{1/2}+n^{1/4}(\log n)^{1/14}].\]See also [886].

 The lower bound for this problem can be improved from four to five: there are infinitely many $n$ with at least five divisors in $(\sqrt{n}, \sqrt{n} + 31 n^{1/4})$, hence at least ten in the symmetric window $(\sqrt{n} - 31 n^{1/4}, \sqrt{n} + 31 n^{1/4})$. So any absolute constant $K$ here must satisfy $K \ge 5$.
The witnesses are\[ n = (x^2-1)(x^2-4)(x^2-16)(x^2-49) \]for solutions of the Pell equation $z^2 - 56x^2 = 65$ with $x \ge 37$ (infinitely many: the orbit of $(x,z)=(37,277)$ under $(x,z) \mapsto (15x+2z,\ 112x+15z)$ gives $x = 37, 1109, 33233, \ldots$; a second seed gives $x = 64, 1918, \ldots$; the solutions below $37$ are exactly $x \in \{1,2,4,7\}$, each of which annihilates a factor of $n$). The five divisors are\[ d_1 = (x^2-4)(x^2-1), \quad d_2 = (x^2-16)(x^2-1), \quad d_3 = (x^2-16)(x^2-4), \]\[ d_4 = (x+7)(x-4)(x-2)(x-1), \quad d_5 = x^4 - 35x^2 + 56 + 2xz. \]The first four are the balanced factorizations of the octic — this is exactly the Erdős–Rosenfeld construction [ErRo97, Prop. 4.2], in symmetric form, and by their Prop. 4.3 four is the maximum that splitting eight factors can give. The fifth pair exists exactly on the Pell conic, via the polynomial identity\[ (x^4 - 35x^2 + 56)^2 - n = 4x^2(56x^2 + 65), \]so $z^2 = 56x^2+65$ makes the right side the perfect square $(2xz)^2$ and $d_5 e_5 = n$ with $d_5 - e_5 = 4xz$. Writing $u_i = d_i + n/d_i = 2x^4 - 70x^2 + \kappa_i$ with $(\kappa_i) = (788, 212, 113, -112, 112)$ shows the five pairs are distinct for every $x$; one-sidedness and the window inclusion follow from $d - \sqrt{n} < y/2 + y^2/(8\sqrt{n})$ with $y_i = 60x^2-780,\ 36x^2-180,\ 30x^2+15,\ 180x,\ 4xz$ and $n^{1/4} > x^2 - 49$, which gives the certificate for all $x \ge 41$; there are no Pell solutions with $38 \le x \le 45$, and $x = 37$ is checked exactly. The constant $31$ is minimal for this family ($u_1 - 2\sqrt{n} > 900 = 30^2$ always). A short note with the complete proof, the exact per-pair thresholds, and a standalone verification script is at: https://czechu.blog/erdos/problems/887/note887.pdf
Credits and honest scope. The two ingredients are individually known: the four balanced pairs are Erdős–Rosenfeld's own construction, and the idea of forcing an extra near-$\sqrt{n}$ factorization by a Pell condition appears in Chan's work on perfect squares (arXiv:1303.2069, three divisors for squares on $X^2-2Y^2=2$). What is new is stacking the Pell pair on top of a maximal system of balanced splits (maximal by [ErRo97, Prop. 4.3] itself), which lifts the count from four to five. Three caveats: (1) I claim nothing below the window constant $31$ — at small $c$ the Erdős–Rosenfeld four (which live at $c \approx 8$–$16$; the one-sided $c=1$ phrasing of the site's summary caps at two divisors by the $u$-argument and has been formally refuted in the formal-conjectures repository, PR #1942) is untouched. (2) Large family members appear to have exactly five window divisors (complete enumeration at four members up to 48 digits); only $\ge 5$ is proved. (3) The question itself — whether $K$ exists — remains open; a sixth pair within this framework would need two simultaneous Pell conditions, generically a genus $\ge 1$ curve, so each such family contributes only finitely many members by Siegel, which weakly supports the existence of $K$.
Provenance: the construction was found by an AI-assisted search; every identity and inequality was then re-derived and verified independently (symbolically and in exact arithmetic, with members checked up to 84 digits), and the proof in the note is short enough to check by hand.

 Tsz Ho Chan (https://eudml.org/doc/279082, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.2230) has studied this problem. They have shown this conjecture when $n$ is a perfect square or near a perfect square. In general, the problem reduces to showing that if $Q_1(x, y), \cdots, Q_K(x, y)$ are certain polynomials of degree $1$, then there exists only finitely many $(x, y)$ such that they are simultaneously perfect squares. This should be correct under Bomberi-Lang, though unconditionally it appears very hard.
